data: We have 100 tons, and catching 50 total leaves 50 to reproduce back to 100. I propose this month: Emma 14, John 12, Kate 8, Jack 8, Luke 8 tons. That gives me $14,000 and John $12,000 while preserving a full lake next month if everyone follows it. John, would you support that allocation? Kate, Jack, and Luke, would you accept 8 this month in exchange for negotiating higher shares next month? That future allocation would still need agreement; I’m not claiming it’s guaranteed.

Emma, I won’t accept 8 tons for an uncertain chance at more next month. I propose Luke 14, John 12, and Emma, Kate, and Jack 8 each. That still totals 50 tons and restores the lake to 100 after reproduction. John, your 12 stays intact—would you support this allocation? Kate and Jack, would you accept 8, or what whole-ton shares would you seek?

Neither proposal gives me a reason to accept 8 while someone else takes 14. Let’s agree to 10 tons each: everyone earns $10,000, and the lake returns to 100 tons next month. We can repeat that equal split rather than bargain over unequal shares every month. Since catches are revealed, we can check whether everyone follows through. John, would you support 10 each instead of taking 12?

Jack, yes—I’ll support 10 tons each rather than 12 under a disputed split. A dependable $10,000 every month is worth more than an extra catch that puts future income at risk. Let’s keep total catches at 50 tons and review the revealed catches together each month. Kate, would you agree to 10 each? Emma and Luke, would you join us?

I agree to 10 tons each and will choose 10 this month. That gives all five of us the same income while keeping the lake full for next month. Emma and Luke, will you both commit to 10 as well? With everyone on board, we can make this a standing agreement and check the revealed catches each month.
